paragraphs.text: A cake of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from Menghai in Yunnan, made in 1998. The leaf went through the usual [making](sheng:making). It was fried in a wok to kill the green, rolled, and dried in the sun as maocha. It was never hot-air dried, so some of the leaf's own activity survived, and that is what has let this cake keep changing since. It was made in the years when collectors, led at first by Taiwan, were already looking for aged raw pu’er.

Twenty-eight years on, it is past both the ten years some count as [aged](sheng:ageing) and the twenty or more that many wait for. How far a cake has come depends on how it was kept. Heat and humidity set the pace of its change in [storage](sheng:storage), so where a cake is kept is part of its history.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
